question:
Consider the function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ defined by $f(n)=n+2$.

(i) Determine whether $1$ and $2$ have pre-images under $f$.

(ii) Hence examine whether $f$ is onto.
explanation:
(i) Pre-image of $1$
If $f(n)=1$, then
$$n+2=1\Rightarrow n=-1.$$
Since $-1\notin\mathbb{N}$, $1$ has no pre-image.

Pre-image of $2$
If $f(n)=2$, then
$$n+2=2\Rightarrow n=0.$$
Since $0\notin\mathbb{N}$, $2$ has no pre-image.

(ii) Onto criterion
An onto function must provide a pre-image in the domain for every element of the co-domain.

Conclusion
Since $1$ and $2$ have no pre-images in $\mathbb{N}$, $f$ is not onto.

options.A: $1$ has no pre-image, $2$ has the pre-image $0$, and $f$ is onto
options.B: Neither $1$ nor $2$ has a pre-image in $\mathbb{N}$, and $f$ is not onto
options.C: Both $1$ and $2$ have pre-images in $\mathbb{N}$, and $f$ is onto
options.D: Neither $1$ nor $2$ has a pre-image in $\mathbb{N}$, but $f$ is onto
